# Candakumārajātaka (Ja 544)

**ID:** Ja 544
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Candakumārajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Prince Moon
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja544
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Candakumārajātaka* (also widely known in the Sri Lankan and Fausbøll manuscript traditions as the *Khandahālajātaka*, numbered Ja 542 in the PTS edition) is one of the celebrated stories of the *Mahānipāta* [Fausböll 1897; Appleton 2010]. In Southeast Asian traditions and modern digital recensions like SuttaCentral, it is numbered Ja 544 and titled after the Bodhisatta, Prince Canda (Candakumāra), rather than the villainous royal priest Khandahāla [Appleton 2010; SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional framing blurb, the Buddha recounted this story while dwelling on Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa) concerning Devadatta, linked to the disruption of the monastic community [SuttaCentral].

The central narrative recounts how King Ekarāja of Pupphavatī, misled by his corrupt Brahman purohita Khandahāla, attempts a massive sacrificial slaughter to attain heaven, lining up his own royal children—including Prince Canda—wives, and domestic animals for sacrifice [Appleton 2014; Luce et al. 1970]. When the sacrificial victims are miraculously delivered, the story strongly condemns animal and human sacrifice, depicting animal slaughter as leading to rebirth in hell [Appleton 2014]. In the *Cariyāpiṭaka* and *Jātakanidānakathā*, Prince Canda is cited as a preeminent exemplar of the Bodhisatta’s perfection of generosity (*dānapāramī*) [Endo 1997; Gaffney 2003; Hazra 1994], while thematic studies also highlight his demonstration of forbearance (*khanti*) in enduring his father's actions [Appleton 2010]. In Burmese Buddhist art and epigraphy, such as at Pagan, the text is depicted through labelled narrative panels [Luce et al. 1970].

According to DharmaNexus, the Pali text shares 171 segments with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (volume 7) and shares shorter passages with the *Candakinnarījātaka* (Ja 485) and *Cūḷasutasomajātaka* (Ja 525) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language machine alignments link portions of the narrative to northern Buddhist texts, notably Kṣemendra’s *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* (D4155-2), the *Jātakamālā* (D4150), and the *Vinayavastu* (D0001-3) [DharmaNexus].

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for ja544 — Supplied Pali title, English translation title 'Prince Moon', and Nidāna framing summary.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus database alignment for ja544 — Identified Pali internal text reuse in the commentary and other Jātakas, as well as Tibetan/Sanskrit cross-language alignments.
- [Appleton 2010] Naomi Appleton, Jātaka Stories in Theravada Buddhism: Narrating the Bodhisatta Path (2010) — Discussed title changes between Southeast Asian and PTS recensions (Candakumāra vs. Khandahāla) and the Bodhisatta's khanti.
- [Appleton 2014] Naomi Appleton, Narrating Karma and Rebirth: Buddhist and Jain Multi-life Stories (2014) — Detailed the narrative critique of animal and human sacrifice in Khandahāla-/Candakumāra-jātaka.
- [Endo 1997] Toshiichi Endo, Buddha in Theravada Buddhism: A Study of the Concept of Buddha in the Pali Commentaries (1997) — Noted Candakumāra's role in illustrating dānapāramī in the Jātaka commentary.
- [Fausböll 1897] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with Its Commentary, Vol. 7 (Index) (1897) — Documented alternative titling and character entry for Candakumāra-jātaka.
- [Gaffney 2003] Sean D. Gaffney, The Jātakanidānakathā: A Critical Study (2003) — Referenced the perfection of perfections at the time of Candakumāra in the Nidānakathā.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Noted Candakumāra's inclusion in the Cariyāpiṭaka's dānapāramī section.
- [Luce et al. 1970] Gordon H. Luce, Bo-Hmu Ba Shin, and U Tin Oo, Old Burma—Early Pagán, Vol. 2 (1970) — Recorded Burmese glosses and narrative representations of the Candakumāra/Khandahāla story.
- [Matilal et al. 1980] Bimal Krishna Matilal et al. (eds.), Sanskrit and Indian Studies (1980) — Discussed Khandahāla's role as purohita in the Candakumāra story.
